periods.activity_title: Tracing the Quilt Border: What Is Perimeter?

tasks_in_class.description: Tick the lace option (red 40 units / green 50 units / blue 25 units) that would cover the entire border of the quilt.
Find the perimeter of the following shapes. All sides of the following shapes are equal. (pentagon with 4 cm side; bowtie figure with 5 cm side)
Draw two rectangles each having the following perimeters. (a) 26 cm (b) 18 cm

time_bands.activity: Introduce the quilt-border context. Students examine the border of the quilt picture and discuss what 'going all the way around' means. The class settles on perimeter as the total length of the boundary of any closed shape.

Opening context, p.142 ("Tick the lace option that would cover the entire border...."). Students reason about which length of lace is enough — not too short, not wastefully long — and justify their choice.

Let Us Do Q1, p.142 ("Find the perimeter of the following shapes. All sides...."). Students count sides, multiply side-length by the number of sides, and record perimeters for the pentagon and the bowtie figure.

Let Us Do Q2, p.142 ("Draw two rectangles each having the following perimeters...."). Students choose length and breadth pairs that sum to half the given perimeter, draw the rectangles on squared paper, and share the variety of rectangles the class produced from the same perimeter.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse perimeter with area at this stage; insisting that they trace the boundary with a finger before computing helps keep the idea concrete. The reverse task — drawing rectangles for a given perimeter — reveals that many different rectangles share the same perimeter, a seed for later comparison. Watch for students who simply double one dimension instead of finding pairs that sum to half the perimeter.

section_titles: Area via tiling — covering regions with shapes
periods.activity_title: Covering Without Gaps: Discovering Area Through Tiling

tasks_in_class.description: Cover your table with triangles, circles, squares, and rectangles. Fill in blanks: which shapes cover without gaps, which leave gaps; count triangles / squares / rectangles covering each table; state the area in triangle / square / rectangle units.

Try to cover the top of your table without gaps and overlaps with the following objects of same size: (a) Notebooks (b) Lunch boxes (c) Pencil boxes (d) Maths textbooks. Which covered the region completely?
Count how many square patches the grandmother used to make the rug shown in the picture.

time_bands.activity: Brief whole-class discussion: 'What does it mean to cover a surface completely?' Students predict which classroom objects — triangles, circles, squares, rectangles — will cover without gaps.

Tiling exploration, p.143 ("Cover your table with triangles, circles, squares, and rectangles...."). Groups place cut-out shapes on their desktops, observe where gaps appear, count tiles that cover completely, and fill in the blanks together.

Table cover with objects, p.143 ("Try to cover the top of your table without gaps...."). Groups use notebooks, lunch boxes, pencil boxes, and maths textbooks and report which objects tile perfectly — connecting classroom objects to the abstract idea of a tiling unit.

Rug patch count, p.143 ("Count how many square patches the grandmother used...."). Students count patches on the printed rug, practising systematic row-by-row counting as a bridge toward the formula to come.

periods.teacher_notes: The key insight here is that area requires a tile that covers without gaps or overlaps, which is why circles fail. Encourage groups to articulate why circles leave gaps rather than simply recording the result. The patch-counting task benefits from a count-by-rows strategy; if students count randomly, gently redirect them to count one row and ask how many rows there are.
materials: Cut-out shapes: equilateral triangles, circles, squares, rectangles (one set per group)
Students' own notebooks, lunch boxes, pencil boxes, maths textbooks

section_titles: Comparing areas using grids and the unit square
periods.activity_title: Palms, Leaves, and Grids: Measuring Area With Unit Squares

tasks_in_class.description: Trace rectangles A, B, C on to a paper and cut them to find out which one has the largest area.
Compare the areas of the two gardens given below on the square grid. Share your observations. Area of Garden A = ___ cm square; Area of Garden B = ___ cm square.
Trace your palm on the square grid and find the approximate area of your palm. Compare the area of your palm with your friend's palm. Who has a bigger palm?
Collect leaves of different kinds. Put them on a square grid and find their area. (a) Name the leaf with the largest area. (b) Name the leaf with the smallest area.

homework.description: The following mats are made of square patches of equal size. How many square patches will be required to cover each mat? Would both mats require an equal or different number of patches? Trace and cut out a small square of the size given and find the area.

time_bands.activity: Trace and cut rectangles, p.144 ("Trace rectangles A, B, C on to a paper and cut them...."). Students trace, cut, and overlap the three rectangles to rank them by area — a hands-on check before any counting begins.

Let Us Do Q1, p.145 ("Compare the areas of the two gardens given below on the square grid...."). Students count unit squares inside each garden outline, record the two areas, and share observations about which garden is larger and by how many unit squares.

Let Us Do Q2, p.146 ("Trace your palm on the square grid...."). Students trace their palm, count full squares and decide how to handle partial squares, then compare with a neighbour's tracing — introducing approximate area for irregular shapes.

Let Us Do Q3, p.146 ("Collect leaves of different kinds. Put them on a square grid...."). Students place collected leaves on the grid, count unit squares, and rank leaves by area, naming the largest and smallest. The teacher highlights that the same counting strategy works for any shape placed on a grid.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often struggle with partial squares when tracing palms or leaves; guide them to count a partial square as one whole square if it is more than half covered, and ignore it otherwise — this is the standard approximation the chapter uses. The trace-and-cut activity anchors the idea that direct comparison (overlap) and grid-counting give consistent rankings. Let Us Do Q4 at p.147 (the mats with square patches) makes a suitable extension for students to try at home.
materials: Squared grid paper (one sheet per student)
A variety of collected leaves (students bring in advance or teacher provides)

section_titles: Comparing areas using grids and the unit square
Area and perimeter relationship — same area, different perimeter
periods.activity_title: Same Area, Different Border: Separating Two Measurements

tasks_in_class.description: Look at the different tiles on Preetha's desk and answer how many of the following shapes will cover the desk. (a) Green triangles (b) Red triangles (c) Blue squares
Tick the shapes with the same area. Find the perimeters of these shapes. What do you notice? Discuss.
Tick the shapes with the same perimeter. Find the areas of these shapes. What do you notice? Discuss.
Draw different shapes having the same area as the given shape. Write the perimeter of each shape. What do you notice? Discuss.

homework.description: Is the area of shape (a) less than the area of shape (b) given below? Discuss.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do (tiles), p.144 ("Look at the different tiles on Preetha's desk...."). Students reason about how many green triangles, red triangles, and blue squares cover the same desk — building the understanding that the same area can be expressed in different tile units.

Let Us Explore Q1, p.147 ("Tick the shapes with the same area. Find the perimeters...."). Students identify equal-area shapes on the grid, compute each perimeter, and notice that equal areas do not guarantee equal perimeters.

Let Us Explore Q2, p.148 ("Tick the shapes with the same perimeter. Find the areas...."). Students now reverse the investigation: equal-perimeter shapes are identified, their areas counted, and students notice that equal perimeters do not guarantee equal areas.

Let Us Do Q1, p.149 ("Draw different shapes having the same area as the given shape...."). Students draw at least two differently shaped figures on the grid that each contain the same number of unit squares as the given rectangle, then measure and record each perimeter, confirming that perimeters differ.

periods.teacher_notes: The central misconception to address here is that a bigger perimeter means a bigger area or vice versa. The two Let Us Explore tasks are deliberately paired to make both directions of independence visible — teach them back to back and draw a class summary on the board contrasting the two. Let Us Do Q2 at p.150, comparing a square and a non-rectangular shape, works well as follow-up practice at home.

section_titles: Area formula for rectangles and squares
periods.activity_title: Rows and Columns: Deriving Area = Length × Breadth

tasks_in_class.description: Find the area of your classroom floor in square meters. Take the help of your teacher to measure the length and breadth of the floor. What is the perimeter of the classroom floor?
Find the area and perimeter of the following shapes (a)–(e) shown on a 1 cm square grid.
Find the area of a rectangular field whose length is 42 m and breadth is 34 m.

homework.description: Find the area and perimeter of the following objects. Use a scale or measuring tape to find the length and the breadth: (1) Cover of the Notebook (2) Newspaper (3) Blackboard (4) Ludo board (5–6 student choice).

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a small rectangle on the board, shades unit squares row by row, and asks: 'Instead of counting every square, what faster method could we use?' Students articulate that rows × columns = total, arriving at Area = Length × Breadth and the parallel formula Area = Length × Length for squares.

Let Us Do Q1, p.151 ("Find the area of your classroom floor in square meters...."). With teacher assistance, two students measure the classroom length and breadth using a tape; the class applies the formula and also calculates the perimeter using 2 × (L + B).

Let Us Do Q2, p.152 ("Find the area and perimeter of the following shapes (a)–(e)...."). Students work individually on the grid-drawn shapes, applying Area = L × B and the perimeter formula, then compare answers in pairs.

Let Us Do Q4, p.153 ("Find the area of a rectangular field whose length is 42 m...."). Students apply the formula to a bare-number word problem — no grid support — consolidating symbolic-level computation.

periods.teacher_notes: The derivation moment (rows × columns) is the conceptual hinge of the chapter; do not rush past it. Students who have counted patches in the tiling and grid sections recognise the shortcut readily. A common error is to add length and breadth instead of multiplying — keep the grid visible on the board while students attempt Q4 so they can self-check by visualising rows. Let Us Do Q3 at p.153 (measuring real objects) extends practice naturally at home.
materials: Measuring tape (at least one, for classroom measurement)

section_titles: Area formula for rectangles and squares
periods.activity_title: Working Backwards and Building Composite Shapes

tasks_in_class.description: The area of a rectangular garden is 64 square m and its length is 16 m. What is its breadth?
Find the area of the following figure with the dimensions as marked in the figure. (L-shaped figure: total width 32 cm, top strip height 6 cm, lower portion height 12 cm)

time_bands.activity: Brief oral warm-up: teacher states three area and perimeter problems; students call out answers to verify the formula Area = L × B is secure before moving to reverse reasoning.

Let Us Do Q5, p.153 ("The area of a rectangular garden is 64 square m and its length is 16 m...."). Teacher models the reverse approach: Area ÷ Length = Breadth, using the idea that multiplication and division are inverse operations. Students then solve independently and verify by multiplying back.

Let Us Do Q6, p.153 ("Find the area of the following figure with the dimensions as marked...."). Students study the L-shaped figure, decide how to split it into two rectangles, label each part's dimensions, compute the two areas, and add them. Groups share their decomposition strategies — some may split horizontally, others vertically.

periods.teacher_notes: Working backwards from area to a missing dimension is a new reasoning direction; if students are stuck, prompt them with 'what multiplication fact gives 64 with one factor of 16?' rather than stating the division. The L-shaped figure is the first composite figure in the chapter and students sometimes mis-read the shared dimensions; insist they label every sub-rectangle before calculating. This unit closes the formula-application work and leaves students ready to use perimeter reasoning flexibly in the game context.
materials: Squared paper (for students who want to sketch the L-shape)

periods.activity_title: Roll, Build, Win: The Perimeter Game With Square Tiles

tasks_in_class.description: Take square tiles and a die. Roll the die, pick tiles equal to dots, arrange to make a shape, find the perimeter. Take turns adding tiles to the same figure till the perimeter becomes 24. The one who makes perimeter 24 wins.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates the game with one volunteer: roll the die, pick that many tiles, arrange them on the desk, count the perimeter aloud. Class discusses why two different arrangements of the same tiles can have different perimeters — sharing more sides reduces the exposed boundary.

Let Us Play, p.154 ("Take square tiles and a die. Roll the die, pick tiles equal to dots...."). Pairs play two full rounds, recording the perimeter after each player's turn on a simple table. The teacher circulates, prompting 'How could you arrange these tiles to get a smaller perimeter? A larger one?'

Class discussion: students share arrangements that increased the perimeter and ones that decreased it. A few pairs demonstrate on the board, and the class generalises that tiles sharing more sides lower the perimeter — connecting the game strategy to the geometry.
Quick closing reflection: each student writes one sentence in their notebook — 'Sharing more sides between tiles makes the perimeter go ___' — to consolidate the insight in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes assume that adding more tiles always increases the perimeter; the game's strategic element forces them to test this belief. Encourage players to try both a line arrangement and a compact cluster arrangement with the same tiles and compare perimeters before locking in a move. The written sentence at the close anchors a genuine generalisation about perimeter and area independence in a form the student can revisit.
materials: A standard six-sided die (one per pair)

items.section_title: Area via tiling — covering regions with shapes
items.prompt: Priya wants to cover her table completely using identical shapes. Which shape will cover the table without any gaps?

options.label: A
options.text: Circles

options.label: B
options.text: Ovals

options.label: C
options.text: Squares

options.label: D
options.text: Triangles with curved sides

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Squares. Squares tile perfectly with no gaps or overlaps.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the shape can fit edge-to-edge with no leftover space.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not yet noticed that curved shapes leave crescent-shaped gaps at every join.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be confusing triangle type; curved-sided triangles cannot tile.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not distinguished between shapes that pack neatly and those that leave gaps.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student physically place cut-out circles and squares on paper to see gaps. Stretch: ask them to draw one more shape that would also tile.

exercise.description: Cover your table with triangles, circles, squares, and rectangles. Fill in blanks: which shapes cover without gaps, which leave gaps; count triangles / squares / rectangles covering each table; state the area in triangle / square / rectangle units.

items.section_title: Comparing areas using grids and the unit square
items.prompt: Trace your hand on the square grid on p.146 and count the unit squares to find the approximate area of your hand. Write the area in unit squares.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Answers will vary by student. The student should count full squares completely inside the tracing, treat squares more than half covered as one whole unit, and ignore the rest. A typical child's hand at Grade V covers approximately 50–80 unit squares on a 1 cm grid.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count full unit squares inside the outline; count a square as whole if more than half is covered.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: teacher marks a few clearly full squares and a few clearly partial ones so the student practises the counting rule before tackling the whole tracing. Stretch: ask the student to compare their hand area with a classmate's and state the difference in unit squares.

exercise.description: Trace your palm on the square grid and find the approximate area of your palm. Compare the area of your palm with your friend's palm. Who has a bigger palm?

items.section_title: Comparing areas using grids and the unit square
items.prompt: A student traced three rectangles P, Q, and R on grid paper and cut them out. She stacked them to compare. Which action would correctly tell her which rectangle has the largest area?

options.label: A
options.text: Count only the squares along the top row of each rectangle.

options.label: B
options.text: Measure only the length of each rectangle.

options.label: C
options.text: Place one rectangle over another to see which one sticks out the most.

options.label: D
options.text: Place the rectangles side by side and see which looks widest.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Place one rectangle over another to see which one sticks out the most. Direct overlap comparison reveals which shape covers more region.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Overlap (trace-and-cut) directly compares covered region without counting.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is confusing width (one dimension) with area (two-dimensional region).
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is confusing length with area; length alone does not determine the region covered.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student counts only one row, missing the contribution of all rows to the total area.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student physically cut out two rectangles of different shapes and overlay them. Stretch: ask whether two rectangles could have the same area even if one is longer — can they draw an example?

exercise.description: Trace rectangles A, B, C on to a paper and cut them to find out which one has the largest area.

items.prompt: A square garden has each side equal to 9 m. Ravi wants to put a fence all around it. How many metres of fencing does he need?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 36 m. Perimeter of a square = 4 × side = 4 × 9 = 36 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the side length by the number of sides: 4 × 9 = 36.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student added only two sides (9 + 9 = 18), forgetting the other two sides.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student multiplied 9 × 9 = 81, computing area instead of perimeter.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student added three sides (9 × 3 = 27), missing one side of the square.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw the square and mark each side before adding. Stretch: ask what happens to the perimeter if one side is doubled — can they predict and verify?

exercise.description: Tick the lace option (red 40 units / green 50 units / blue 25 units) that would cover the entire border of the quilt.

items.prompt: Draw a rectangle on your grid paper that has a perimeter of 20 cm. Write down the length and breadth you chose. Can you draw a different rectangle that also has a perimeter of 20 cm? Write its length and breadth.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any pair of whole-number dimensions (L, B) where L + B = 10 is correct. Possible answers include 6 cm × 4 cm, 7 cm × 3 cm, 8 cm × 2 cm, 9 cm × 1 cm, or 5 cm × 5 cm. Two different valid rectangles must be given.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Half the perimeter (10 cm) is split into a length–breadth pair; any pair summing to 10 is valid.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: tell the student that half the perimeter is 10 and ask them to find two numbers that add to 10. Stretch: ask how many different rectangles with whole-number sides can have a perimeter of 20 cm, and which one would have the largest area.

exercise.description: Draw two rectangles each having the following perimeters. (a) 26 cm (b) 18 cm

items.section_title: Comparing areas using grids and the unit square
items.prompt: Look at the two shapes below drawn on a square grid. Count the unit squares in each and write which shape has the larger area. By how many unit squares is it larger?
items.visual_stimulus:
| Shape | Number of unit squares |
| Shape X | 12 |
| Shape Y | 9 |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Shape X has the larger area. It has 12 unit squares and Shape Y has 9 unit squares, so Shape X is larger by 3 unit squares.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count unit squares inside each outline and subtract the smaller count from the larger.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to colour each unit square as they count so no square is missed or counted twice. Stretch: ask them to sketch a shape on the grid that has an area between 9 and 12 unit squares.

exercise.description: Compare the areas of the two gardens given below on the square grid. Share your observations. Area of Garden A = ___ cm square; Area of Garden B = ___ cm square.

items.section_title: Area and perimeter relationship — same area, different perimeter
items.prompt: Two shapes on a grid each have an area of 8 unit squares. Meena says their perimeters must also be equal. Is she right?

options.label: A
options.text: No, shapes with the same area can have different perimeters.

options.label: B
options.text: Only if both shapes are rectangles.

options.label: C
options.text: Only if both shapes are squares.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, equal areas always mean equal perimeters.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No, shapes with the same area can have different perimeters. A 1 × 8 rectangle and a 2 × 4 rectangle both have area 8 unit squares but perimeters of 18 and 12 respectively.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count unit squares for area and add up boundary edges for perimeter — they are independent.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not yet separated the two attributes; they believe area determines perimeter.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student partially grasps the idea but incorrectly restricts it to rectangles only.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student restricts the independence to squares only, missing the general principle.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw two different shapes that both have 6 unit squares and then count each perimeter. Stretch: ask them to find the arrangement of 8 unit squares that gives the smallest possible perimeter.

exercise.description: Tick the shapes with the same area. Find the perimeters of these shapes. What do you notice? Discuss.

items.section_title: Area and perimeter relationship — same area, different perimeter
items.prompt: Two shapes on a grid have the same perimeter of 12 units. Do they necessarily have the same area? Draw two different shapes on grid paper that each have a perimeter of 12 units, count their areas, and write what you notice.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No, equal perimeters do not mean equal areas. For example, a 1 × 5 rectangle has perimeter 12 and area 5 unit squares, while a 3 × 3 square has perimeter 12 and area 9 unit squares. Any two valid examples with perimeter 12 and different areas are acceptable.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find pairs of dimensions summing to 6 (half the perimeter) and compute L × B for each.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student one worked example (a 1 × 5 rectangle) and ask them to draw just one more shape with the same perimeter. Stretch: ask which perimeter-12 shape has the largest area and how they can be sure.

exercise.description: Tick the shapes with the same perimeter. Find the areas of these shapes. What do you notice? Discuss.

items.section_title: Area and perimeter relationship — same area, different perimeter
items.prompt: On your grid paper, the given rectangle has an area of 10 unit squares. Draw two different shapes that also have an area of 10 unit squares. Write the perimeter of each shape you drew. What do you notice about the perimeters?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any two shapes covering exactly 10 unit squares with different perimeters are correct. For example, a 2 × 5 rectangle (perimeter 14) and a 1 × 10 rectangle (perimeter 22) both have area 10 but different perimeters. Students should state that the perimeters differ even though the areas are equal.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count squares to confirm area = 10, then count boundary edges for each perimeter.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: suggest the student try a 1 × 10 strip as their first shape and count its perimeter carefully. Stretch: challenge them to find the shape with 10 unit squares that has the smallest possible perimeter.

exercise.description: Draw different shapes having the same area as the given shape. Write the perimeter of each shape. What do you notice? Discuss.

items.prompt: Anil has 4 square tiles. He can arrange them in a straight line (1 × 4) or in a 2 × 2 block. Which arrangement gives the smaller perimeter?

options.label: A
options.text: Both arrangements give the same perimeter.

options.label: B
options.text: The 1 × 4 straight line, because it uses more tiles in a row.

options.label: C
options.text: The 2 × 2 block, because the tiles share more sides.

options.label: D
options.text: The perimeter depends on the size of each tile, not the arrangement.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The 2 × 2 block. The 1 × 4 line has perimeter 10 units; the 2 × 2 block has perimeter 8 units. Tiles sharing more internal sides expose fewer boundary edges.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count exposed outer edges: 1 × 4 has 10 outer edges; 2 × 2 has 8 outer edges.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses the number of tiles in a row with perimeter length.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student does not realise that shared internal sides reduce the exposed boundary.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses tile size (a constant here) with the effect of arrangement on perimeter.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw both arrangements on grid paper and count the boundary squares one by one. Stretch: ask what arrangement of 6 tiles gives the smallest perimeter and have them verify.

exercise.description: Take square tiles and a die. Roll the die, pick tiles equal to dots, arrange to make a shape, find the perimeter. Take turns adding tiles to the same figure till the perimeter becomes 24. The one who makes perimeter 24 wins.

items.prompt: A regular hexagon has each side equal to 6 cm. What is its perimeter?

options.label: A
options.text: 12 cm

options.label: B
options.text: 30 cm

options.label: C
options.text: 36 cm

options.label: D
options.text: 42 cm

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 36 cm. A regular hexagon has 6 equal sides: 6 × 6 = 36 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply side length by number of sides: 6 × 6 = 36 cm.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student multiplied by 5 instead of 6, perhaps confusing a hexagon with a pentagon.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student added only two sides (6 + 6 = 12), applying a two-side rule instead of counting all sides.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student multiplied by 7, perhaps miscounting the sides of the hexagon.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw the hexagon, label each side, and add them one by one. Stretch: ask what the perimeter would be if one side were 8 cm and the rest remained 6 cm.

exercise.description: Find the perimeter of the following shapes. All sides of the following shapes are equal. (pentagon with 4 cm side; bowtie figure with 5 cm side)

items.section_title: Area via tiling — covering regions with shapes
items.prompt: A small mat is made of square patches arranged in 5 rows with 6 patches in each row. How many square patches are used in the mat?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count row by row: 5 rows × 6 patches per row = 30 patches.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw the mat on grid paper and count each row separately before totalling. Stretch: ask how many patches would be needed if the mat had one more row.

exercise.description: Count how many square patches the grandmother used to make the rug shown in the picture.

items.section_title: Area formula for rectangles and squares
items.prompt: A rectangle on a 1 cm square grid has a length of 9 cm and a breadth of 5 cm. What is its area in square cm? What is its perimeter in cm?

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw the rectangle on grid paper and count the rows of squares before applying the formula. Stretch: ask them to draw a different rectangle with the same area and find its perimeter.

exercise.description: Find the area and perimeter of the following shapes (a)–(e) shown on a 1 cm square grid.

items.section_title: Area formula for rectangles and squares
items.prompt: A rectangular playground is 38 m long and 25 m wide. What is its area in square metres?

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first estimate by rounding (40 × 25 = 1000) and then compute the exact answer. Stretch: ask for the perimeter of the playground as well.

exercise.description: Find the area of a rectangular field whose length is 42 m and breadth is 34 m.

items.section_title: Area formula for rectangles and squares
items.prompt: The area of a rectangular room is 48 square metres. Its length is 8 m. What is the breadth of the room?

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student which multiplication fact with 8 gives 48, then identify the breadth. Stretch: ask them to find the perimeter of the room using the length and breadth they found.

exercise.description: The area of a rectangular garden is 64 square m and its length is 16 m. What is its breadth?

items.section_title: Area formula for rectangles and squares
items.prompt: An L-shaped figure is made of two rectangles. The top rectangle is 20 cm wide and 5 cm tall. The bottom rectangle is 10 cm wide and 8 cm tall. What is the total area of the L-shaped figure?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 180 sq cm. Top rectangle: 20 × 5 = 100 sq cm. Bottom rectangle: 10 × 8 = 80 sq cm. Total = 100 + 80 = 180 sq cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Split the L-shape into two rectangles, apply Area = L × B to each, then add the two areas.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to sketch the L-shape, draw the dividing line, and label each rectangle's dimensions before calculating. Stretch: ask them to find the perimeter of the whole L-shaped figure using the given dimensions.

exercise.description: Find the area of the following figure with the dimensions as marked in the figure. (L-shaped figure: total width 32 cm, top strip height 6 cm, lower portion height 12 cm)
